title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. Improving the bound by another slowly growing factor would be meaningful progress while leaving the yes/no statement unsettled.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.
why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

importance.reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.

progress.text: Han–Thorup achieve O(n√log log n) expected time and linear space for arbitrary word-sized integer keys.
Han’s journal paper gives deterministic O(n log log n) time and linear space, following STOC 2002.
Belazzougui–Brodal–Nielsen extend expected linear time to w=Ω((log n)² log log n).
The CMU integer-sorting lecture retains linear sorting for arbitrary word lengths as an open question and distinguishes polynomial-size universes.

status_note: The all-word-length Las Vegas linear-time target remains open in the checked sources. The 2014 large-word theorem and ordinary radix sorting leave an intermediate regime; a search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution. The exact primitive-operation and randomness conventions are stated on this card.

sentences: Integer sorting can inspect the bits of keys instead of treating them only as objects to compare.
The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length.
The constant must remain uniform when keys occupy much more than logarithmically many bits.
Ordinary radix sorting handles smaller universes but its number of passes can grow.
This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.
